en: Preface to the Commentary on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, composed by the Kinkō śramaṇa Kyōshū.
In the past, when Great Master Jikaku entered China, he carried with him the commentary on the *Vajracchedikā* by the Jin dynasty master Zhaokong.
It was transmitted and returned [to its source], then hidden within a famous mountain. Its radiance did not illuminate the world for nearly nine hundred years.
Recently, the Zen practitioner Zuofang brought it forth and informed me, saying: "This is the original text brought back by my late master; I have happened upon it.
I request that you, Master, verify it and publish it in woodblocks, so that all who see or hear it may plant the seeds of Prajñā. I accepted it and read it; half of it...
Closing the volume, he sighed and said: "As for this sutra, it is the ninth assembly of the *Prajñāpāramitā*. It directly reveals the subtle principle of generating the mind through non-abiding;
thus it is said to be 'spoken for those who set forth upon the Supreme Vehicle. Indeed, there has never been a bodhisattva who, without studying the *Prajñāpāramitā*, attained unsurpassed bodhi.
Therefore, [the commentaries by] the four great bodhisattvas—Maitreya, Vasubandhu, Asaṅga, and Guṇaprabha—"
Saṃghavarman composed verses and treatises to praise and propagate it, and thus the Dharma flowed into China.
When Kumārajīva first translated it, Master Sengzhao provided a commentary. From that time until now, many have made it their daily practice.

Furthermore, from the "sealing of the mind" at Huangmei to the "awakening to the Way" at Caoxi, no scripture has been as renowned for its spiritual efficacy or as abundant in commentaries as this sutra; yet, regarding its commentary—
Among these ancient [commentaries], that of Master Zhaolun comes first. Regarding the commentary that has arrived from the Far East (*Dàdōng*), this present commentary also precedes it.

That the various commentaries previously in circulation have been surpassed by this one—is this not due to the convergence of time and conditions? The Great Master of Tiantai once lectured on this sutra.

I rely exclusively on Master Zhaokong, just as the *Amitābha Sūtra* relies exclusively on Master Jingying. Therefore, whenever there are errors or points of doubt, I have collated them against the Tiantai commentary.
Alas! This commentary was esteemed and utilized by Tiantai and requested from afar by Cijue. Its language is archaic and its meaning profound;
it deeply captures the Buddha’s intent and is perfectly suited for those of a concise disposition. It is truly a lifeline for those in the ocean of suffering.
It is a ford and a bridge; it is the south-pointing chariot for those lost on their path. If this is carved into wood and put into practice, how great will its benefit be!

Therefore, I have collated this with joy. I also pray that future readers of these commentaries may, by following the finger, find the moon, and realize the subtle meaning of the "mind arising from non-abiding.
Thus, they shall breathe from the same nostrils as those of Huangmei and Caoxi, and there will be no need for further fuss.
Engaging in the divergent theories of later generations, he considered himself erudite.
This is the commentary on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, composed in the summer of the twelfth year of the Bǎolì era, the Renwǔ year.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yaoqin [Dynasty] and annotated by Shi Sengzhao of the Yaoqin [Dynasty].
Now, the principle returns to the Middle Way, taking the Two Truths as its tenet. Why is this? The arising of all phenomena is entirely dependent upon causes and conditions.

That which undergoes arising and ceasing, flux and transformation, being floating, false, and unreal, is termed the "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*). All phenomena produced by causes and conditions lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
since intrinsic nature is absent, causes and conditions are entirely forgotten. Fundamentally unborn, they are now without cessation;

their essence is ultimate and unchanging—this is designated as the "real" (*paramārtha*). These two, the real and the conventional, are dual; when their principle is scrutinized, they are the truths (*satya*). This is the Sage’s mind...
Right contemplation discerns the truth and illuminates the mundane; this is the understanding of the dharma-characteristics of the Middle Way, which is termed *prajñā*.
*Prajñā* is wisdom. "Vajra" is a metaphor for that which is firm and sharp: being firm, nothing can obstruct it; being sharp, there is nothing it does not shatter.
This is used as an analogy for this wisdom: evil and depravity cannot destroy it, for it is the ultimate in firmness. Fundamental afflictions...
"All things are shattered"—this is the meaning of "sharpening" (*li*). "Pāramitā" means "reaching the other shore. Birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is taken as "this," and Nirvana as "that.
The Great Being, riding upon the wisdom of signlessness (*animitta-prajñā*), abandons this birth-and-death and reaches that Nirvana.

It has the sense of a "ford" or "passage" (*tīrtha*); it is said that [wisdom] arises from principle, and principle is manifested through words. The student attains spiritual awakening by following this principle.
The teaching is thus fully understood.
This sutra’s fundamental essence takes the wisdom of emptiness as its primary focus; a brief account of its beginning and end consists of three chapters.

From the opening until the section on "Honoring the Disciples," it clarifies that the objective realm is empty; the intent here lies in describing the realm, without yet speaking of wisdom. The second [chapter] correctly establishes the title.
The "Discourse on Wisdom" (*Prajñāpāramitā*) clarifies that wisdom is empty; it merely speaks of the emptiness of wisdom, yet has not yet reached the practitioner.
From the third section, "The Questions," onwards, it clarifies the emptiness of the Bodhisattva. At the beginning of these three chapters, their respective texts manifest clearly;

while the preceding and following sections are similar in form, their underlying meanings differ. Among the four periods of *prajñā*, this is the very first; its language is concise yet its meaning is profound, and its subtle purport is difficult to perceive.

Venturing to provide annotations for this work despite its rustic and humble nature, I have merely recounted its general outline; it is not intended to exhaustively analyze or investigate its subtle details.
I request that those of clear discernment wait for such a task.
Thus it is.
When the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, his attendant requested, "What should be placed at the beginning of all sūtras?
The Buddha instructed Ānanda: "It should be said: 'Thus [have I heard],' down to 'at that time, the assembly. It is as I have transmitted it; it is as the Buddha spoke it.
It is said thus:
"I have heard.
If it were merely heard from another, it would not necessarily be so; however, I have heard it directly from the golden mouth [of the Buddha], and the matter is not erroneous.

First: This means that one has personally heard what accords with principle; since it does not accord with principle for oneself, what would be the point of transmitting it? If one speaks, it must accord with principle.
Principle. Principle is also like words; since words do not deviate from principle, they are said to be one.
Time. Although it is said that one must accord with principle, one cannot disregard the timing. If the timing is not right, how can one awaken others? The Sage does not... [The text is incomplete.]
These are not empty words; they must accord with the capacities of those present. This is the teaching of the "Right Time.

When the Buddha was in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, the Dharma King moved through the world, traveling in response to sentient beings. At one time, he descended and assembled at the great city of Śrāvastī, in the land of Kośala.
This is the Jetavana Anāthapiṇḍika-ārāma in the kingdom of Rājagṛha.
Sudatta purchased the grove and Jeta offered the trees; together they established the vihāra, and thus it is called "Jetavana Anāthapiṇḍika."
[This was] a garden. (The *Shi shu* [Commentary on the *Sūtra*] reads "cloth" instead of "garden.
Together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
The Sage’s transformation is impartial; those who listen must have their peers. That they all heard as if in a forest makes it clear that this is credible. There must have been four [assemblies].
[This] has been omitted from the *Zhòng* [commentary]. ○ In my private commentary, I have written "secret" (*mì*).

At that time, when the World-Honored One was at his mealtime—having daily prepared his provisions and the food being ready—at such a time, every household possesses [the means], and the intention to give arises easily.
He put on his robes;
he donned the *saṃghāṭī*, the field-of-merit robe (*puṇyakṣetra-cīvara*). The Buddha observed that the furrows of a fertile field were well-aligned and even, and thereupon commanded his attendant:
"Of all fields of merit for those who have left the household life, whenever one fashions a *saṃghāṭī*, this alone shall be used. This is intended to..."

Reflecting upon it, I consider that the Way does not rely on empty offerings. ○ [The character for] *keng* (pit) in the commentary on the *Sheng* (vehicle) is written as *qu* (furrow) and *qeng* (field ridge).
To "hold the bowl" means to grasp the *pātra* (alms-bowl).
He entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
The Dharma-body has no dependencies; what need or desire could it have? Yet, with sublime offerings from humans and devas overflowing daily, he manifested the practice of almsround.
"Merit is appropriate for things. [The current commentary reads "self," but "merit is appropriate for things" should be read as "merit is the appropriateness of things.
Having completed his alms-round sequentially within that city, he returned to his original location.
He did not bypass the poor for the wealthy, nor did he abandon the lowly to follow the noble; his great compassion was impartial, reaching all in due order.
When the meal was finished, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, prepared a seat, and sat down.
When the Prajñāpāramitā was about to be recited, [Śāriputra] respectfully wiped it and spread it out himself.
At that time, the Elder Subhūti, being among the great assembly, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground,
and joined his palms in reverent salutation.
Now, although a divine bell is resonant, it does not ring without being struck; the Sage does not respond in isolation, for shadow and echo follow only virtue.

Because the Master is revered and the Way is weighty, one must therefore exercise utmost reverence and exhaust all courtesy. (Note: In the *Shenzhong shu*, "shenzhong" [divine bell] is written as "juzhong" [great bell]; "kek" [must] is written as "ke" [conquer/overcome].)
He then addressed the Buddha, saying: "How rare, World-Honored One!
The weight of your compassionate grace is beyond words.
The Tathāgata well protects and sustains all bodhisattvas; the Tathāgata well entrusts all bodhisattvas."
"Protective mindfulness" and "entrustment" are truly rare and significant matters. To provide benevolent protection and guidance so that one may carry out the teachings is "protective mindfulness.
To commission and transmit the teachings so that the Way may be established and perfected is "entrustment."

World-Honored One, when good sons and good daughters give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—wherein "bodhi" means omniscience—they set their intent upon and direct themselves toward it, aspiring from afar for perfect enlightenment; therefore, it is said that they "give rise to the mind.
(The *Yìshū* [Commentary on Meaning] writes this as "mind.")
"How should one dwell? How should one subdue the mind?
The sublime fruit of Bodhi is not attained without practice. Although the myriad practices are vast, there are degrees of clarity and obscurity in understanding;

thus, there are distinctions such as 'dwelling' and 'subduing. At the beginning, one suppresses the mind to conform to the principle and gradually trains it through habituation—this is called 'subduing. Ultimately, one can..."
To realize and understand the fundamental principle, with the mind not wavering or departing—this is what is called "abiding.
Regarding the characters for "stage," "doubt," and "abiding," the Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! It is just as you have said:
the Tathāgata skillfully protects and sustains all bodhisattvas, and skillfully entrusts all bodhisattvas."

Regarding the ritual for praising [the Buddhas], one must attend to the capacities of the audience; it is most excellent and perfect, exactly as you have said. ○ All the commentaries treat this as an invitation:
"You should now listen attentively; I shall explain it for you. Son of good family, daughter of good family, those who resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*..."
Regarding the mind of Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, one should abide thus and thus subdue that mind.

If one listens without careful attention, then words will leak out and principles will be lost; therefore, one should cause them to listen attentively so that the words and principles do not become empty.
(The commentary may alternatively render this as "exhortation.")
"Indeed, World-Honored One. We wish and desire to hear it.
May you, out of compassion, grant us leave to speak; we shall listen with reverent gravity and an attentive mind. [The *Jieshu* reads "jie" (admonition) instead of "jie" (precept).
The Buddha told Subhūti: "All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should thus subdue their minds."
One who empties the mind and treads the Way is called a Bodhisattva; one who extensively saves all things is a Mahāsattva.
This should correspond to what is explained below, for that is the method of subduing. Question: Why is the answer given before the question? Answer: [This is because] the subduing occurs later.
Abiding in the profound while descending to the shallow, the questioner first indicates the profound; because descending to the shallow makes it easy to practice, the answer is given beforehand.
There is a specific intent in this sequence of question and answer; it is not an error.
Of all classes of sentient beings—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation;

whether possessing form or formless; whether with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception—I shall cause them all to enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder and bring them to final liberation.
This is the correct answer concerning the practice of subduing. Although the myriad dharmas are vast, they may be briefly categorized into two sections:

first, the dharmas of sentient beings; second, the dharmas of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). Dharmas do not arise of themselves; they arise due to causes and conditions. These causes and conditions, however, lack inherent nature (*svabhāva*) altogether.

This is to understand in accordance with principle; to deviate from this fundamental tenet is to produce delusion. Because of delusion, one wanders through the cycle of birth and death; through understanding, one [attains liberation].

The accumulated [defilements] are extinguished in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Body and mind constitute suffering; the exhaustion of suffering is bliss. The path to exhausting suffering is none other than Great Liberation (*mahā-vimukti*).
When liberation is perfected and delusion is exhausted, body and mind are both forgotten. This state of profound stillness and eternal bliss is called *nirvāṇa*.

Were it not for my extensive transformation [of beings], how could the multitudes of living beings be delivered? Ordinary liberation does not arise spontaneously; it must depend on gradual cultivation. The provisional names and dharmas are merely coarse approximations.
To suppress the mind is easy; therefore, one first proceeds to the emptiness of sentient beings (*sattva-śūnyatā*) to clarify subjugation.
Since all things are non-active and empty, delusion itself is liberation when one realizes that what is created by delusion is itself liberation. Thus, activity is itself [liberation].
In this way, although one brings immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings to parinirvāṇa, in reality there are no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa.

This explains the Middle Way, which is neither existent nor non-existent: because they lack intrinsic nature, they do not exist; yet because they are designated by provisional names, they are not non-existent.
Since it is not that provisional names are absent, one constantly delivers sentient beings; yet because their self-nature is empty, in reality there is no one who attains extinction.
Why is this? Subhūti, if there were the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span, one would not be a bodhisattva.
To explain why there is no cessation: if there were a mark of a self, one could speak of its cessation; since there is neither self nor person, how could there be cessation?
Who is it that extinguishes? It is merely a provisional designation, yet one recklessly conceives of a self. To cling to the self is wrong; to forget the self is right.
Once right and wrong are manifest, gain and loss become clear.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should practice giving without dwelling on any phenomenon. That is to say, they should not dwell on form when practicing giving;
nor should they dwell on sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena when practicing giving.

Next, the answer concerning abiding and practice clarifies the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). This means that phenomena are vast and expansive; to provide a brief illustration, there are the six perfections internally and the six sense objects externally.

All such internal and external phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) because they arise through dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Since they lack intrinsic nature due to dependent origination, the mind has no place to rest;
therefore, one should abide nowhere. To relinquish the mind without stinginess is called giving (*dāna*). There is no characteristic (*nimitta*) to be grasped...
[The text] exists. What is there to begrudge? Giving is the foremost of the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā), and the dust [of the world] is the foundation for the arising of the Dharma.

Both of these dharmas are empty; how could they not be exhausted? Having attained the emptiness of dharmas, one’s understanding becomes clear and practice is established, such that there is no further falling back or loss;
therefore, it is called "abiding. (In the *Ji shu*, "foundation" is written as "mechanism.")
Subhūti, a bodhisattva should give in this manner: not dwelling upon signs.
This concludes the meaning of "dwelling. The giver, the recipient, and the gift are all unapprehendable; thus, one does not dwell upon signs.
Why is this? If a bodhisattva practices giving without dwelling on signs, that merit is inconceivable and immeasurable.
To explain why one should practice giving without dwelling on signs: it is precisely because when one gives with a mind of emptiness, the resulting merit cannot be measured.
Thus, we know that not dwelling on signs is correct, while dwelling on signs is incorrect. Furthermore, since the principle is already immeasurable, the mind [should not dwell].
It should be limited. Because one practices giving in accordance with principle, is it not the case that one's merit becomes even more vast?
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the space in the eastern direction be measured? "No, World-Honored One.
Subhūti, can the space in the southern, western, and northern directions, as well as the four intermediate directions and the zenith and nadir, be measured? "No, World-Honored One."
Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices giving without abiding in signs, their merit is likewise immeasurable and inconceivable.

When the principle reaches its ultimate limit in the two kinds of emptiness, the cessation of abiding becomes manifest. Once both principle and practice are revealed, one should then listen with a concentrated mind and act according to what has been taught;
such merit is vast. To illustrate the extent of this vastness: it is equal to the great void.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva should simply abide as instructed.
The words of the Sage are without error, and the principle cannot be transgressed; one should simply settle the mind according to what the Buddha has taught.
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of his physical marks?

The Bodhisattva’s generation of the mind encompasses three aspects: first, the transformation of sentient beings; second, the cultivation of the myriad practices; and third, the orientation toward Bodhi.
Having already clarified the ritual for transforming beings through the subduing [of the Māras], this chapter demonstrates the path of cultivation through the analysis of the stages of abiding.
This clarifies the method for approaching Bodhi. The physical marks of the Tathāgata’s body are the very substance of Bodhi. If one realizes the *dharmakāya*, then one may ascend to Bodhi;
if one calculates [Bodhi] as being truly existent, one is far removed from it. Therefore, by inquiring about the *dharmakāya*, he clarifies that Bodhi is empty.
(The commentary on "its substance" renders it as "the substance of the fruit"; the commentary on "calculating true Bodhi" renders it as "calculating the nature.")
In reality, the two characters "bodhi" do not exist; therefore, because they are produced through conditioning, he raises this question.
[Subhūti replied: "No, World-Honored One. One cannot see the Tathāgata by means of the marks of the body.
Subhūti has a profound understanding of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya); thus, he says that one cannot see [the Buddha] by means of the actual marks of the physical body. ○
The commentary on the character "real" (*śī*) does not exist [in the original].
Why is this? It explains by citing the Buddha’s own words: "The bodily marks described by the Tathāgata are themselves not bodily marks.
As for the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), it is the ultimate of all virtues; its essence contains all virtues. Sublime.
The body is a composite of aggregations; as its conditioned construction lacks intrinsic nature, it is therefore not a body.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Whatever has marks is entirely false and illusory."
This restates the words of Subhūti. Furthermore, it is empty and false; its principle is not that of characteristics. Moreover, because it is a provisional name, it is empty;
is it then real that one reckons it to be false?
If one sees that all marks are non-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata.
When practice accords with understanding and penetration, then one sees the Buddha.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, are there any sentient beings who, upon hearing such spoken words and phrases as these,"
"Have you given rise to true faith? The principle is empty and signless;

the extraordinary mind has no locus. At that time, my hearing was dim and obscure; it did not immediately take root in my mind. I appeared as though I had not yet awakened, and thus I questioned you in this way.
Now that the teaching is complete, even the Dharma should be relinquished, let alone what is not the Dharma. Thus, one verifies the principle through the body by means of faith."
The *Qishu* (Record of Extraordinary Events) records that the Buddha said: "Subhūti, do not speak thus.
The noble ones do not utter empty words; their realization flows like a stream. How can one then ask whether there is [an object]—what kind of words are these?
After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, during the final five hundred years, there will be those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit;
they will be able to give rise to faith in these words and phrases, regarding them as the truth.
In the final five hundred years, during the period of the Semblance Dharma, humanity will decline and the Way will be lost; yet there will still be those who possess faith.

How much more so now, when the Great Sage has manifested his inspiration, the wise and brilliant gather like clouds, and followers of the transformation are as numerous as a forest—how can one say there is no faith?

That people of future generations will be able to believe requires that they be endowed with the virtue of the precepts. As for those today who have not yet awakened, their lack of merit, folly, and ignorance cause them to create their own doubts and obstructions; this is contrary to principle.
This is not false.
You should know that such a person has not planted roots of goodness under one, two, three, four, or five buddhas;
rather, they have already planted various roots of goodness in the presence of immeasurable thousands of millions of buddhas.
Having seen the Buddha and heard the Dharma, and having accumulated merit for a long time, one is then able to believe in the profound and subtle nature of the Dharma.
Subhūti, when any sentient beings hear these words and phrases and give rise to pure faith, even for a single thought-moment, the Tathāgata knows them all and sees them all;
such sentient beings shall obtain immeasurable merit.
By means of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, it is clear that this principle is not false. A single moment of pure faith brings immeasurable merit.
When one examines its efficacy and fathoms its underlying principle, how could one not believe it?
Why is this? Because these sentient beings no longer possess the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a sentient being, or the notion of a life-span.
Although a single thought-moment is extremely brief, why is its merit immeasurable? It is precisely because they are free from any notions of self or person that their realization is so vast.
There is no mark of dharmas, nor is there any mark of non-dharmas.
There is no mark of dharmas with causes and conditions, nor is there any mark of non-dharmas without causes and conditions.
Why is this? Because if these sentient beings grasp at marks with their minds, they thereby become attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
The arbitrary conceptualization of a self and persons should be forgotten for the sake of principle. All phenomena are principle; why, then, would they not exist?

It is precisely because the mind takes the four great elements as its object and, through conventional designations, conceives of phenomena as "self" and "person," that such views arise. When one perceives the emptiness of these conventional designations, the notions of self and person cease;
therefore, they should indeed be non-existent.
If one grasps at the characteristics of phenomena, one is immediately attached to the notions of self, person, sentient being, and life-span.
If one grasps at the characteristics of real phenomena such as form, sound, and fragrance, one likewise gives rise to views of self, person, and so forth; therefore, these should be absent.
Why is this? If one grasps at the characteristics of non-dharma (*adharma*), one is immediately attached to the notions of self, person, sentient being, and life-span.

[The text asks: Why, then, is there also no non-dharma? Because existence arises in dependence upon emptiness, and because of existence, there is emptiness. If emptiness were without the characteristic of existence, clouds would arise;

by grasping at these arising characteristics as a self, the myriad possibilities of compassion would be born. (Or perhaps "compassion" should be read as "kindness. *Note: The text contains a scribal error where "or kindness" (*huo ci*) appears instead of "or compassion" (*huo ci*).*
This causes confusion.
Therefore, one should not grasp at dharmas, nor should one grasp at non-dharmas;
this includes the binding of the mark of non-existence and the mark of non-non-existence. When both emptiness and existence are forgotten, the mind has nothing to grasp. Thus it is explained.
They realize equality; the fetters are exhausted and the Path is accomplished.
For this reason, the Tathāgata has constantly said: "O bhikṣus, understand my teaching of the Dharma as being like the simile of the raft."
"Even the Dharma should be relinquished, how much more so that which is not Dharma.
This cites a former teaching to corroborate the present principle. It is like one who wishes to cross a river and constructs a raft to carry themselves across;

once they have reached the other shore, they abandon the raft and depart. So too, when seeking to transcend birth and death, one provisionally relies upon the myriad practices; once one has arrived at Nirvana, the myriad [practices]...
It is well that even equanimity is relinquished; if even the dharmas of the Path are to be relinquished, how much more so the emptiness of what is not the Dharma.
[The two characters "of emptiness" (之空) are absent from the commentary. Subhūti, what do you think? Has the Tathāgata attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
"Has the Tathāgata preached any Dharma?
Thus he ultimately honored his disciples, citing the shared realization of the noble ones to prove the necessity of this principle.
Subhūti said: "As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has preached, there is no fixed dharma that can be called 'Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi'."
In *samyaksambodhi*, there is likewise no fixed dharma that the Tathāgata could speak of.
As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, the exhaustion of all marks is called bodhi. Because it is markless, it does not exist;
because it is a provisional name, it is not non-existent. Since it is neither existent nor non-existent, what reality could be attained? What could be fixed?
It can be spoken of. Regarding the character following "exhausting" (qióng), there is doubt as to whether it should be "liberation" (tuō) or "explanation" (jiě).
Why is this? For all the teachings spoken by the Tathāgata are ungraspable and unspeakable.
Awakening has no characteristic that can be grasped; all phenomena are empty and ineffable. Therefore, they possess no fixed reality.
They are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas.
Because they are not dharmas, they do not exist; because they are not non-dharmas, they are not non-existent. Both existence and non-existence are absent—this is the ultimate principle.
Regarding the four characters "Because it exists, it cannot be said" above the section on existence and non-existence:
why is this? It is because all worthy ones and sages are distinguished by means of the dharma of non-activity (asaṃskṛta-dharma).
In principle, there is neither arising nor ceasing; this is called the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). This principle of the unconditioned is understood identically by all the sages.

By realizing and comprehending the unconditioned, the fetters are exhausted and the Path is perfected—this is what is meant by the single meaning of liberation, wherein all equally enter into the *dharmatā*.

Nevertheless, although the unconditioned is one, there are degrees of clarity and obscurity in its realization; differences in excellence arise from whether this clarity is profound or shallow, and whether it is deep or superficial.

"Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would the merit obtained by that person be great? Subhūti replied, "It would be very great, World-Honored One."
Furthermore, regarding the sublation of merit: it is precisely because the principle is clear that merit is so great, and for this reason, it is appropriate to propagate it.
Why is this? This merit is not the nature of merit; therefore, the Tathāgata says that the merit is great.
Merit has no inherent nature; it can be increased through causes and conditions. Because it is easily diminished when it becomes excessive, I have therefore sent it away.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Venerable Subhūti, as well as the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās,
and all the world— including gods, humans, and asuras— having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly filled with joy.

Believing and accepting, they practiced accordingly. The Way was stored within their holy minds; it manifested when the time for its fulfillment arrived. Past karmic responses were secretly formed, gathering without prior consultation.
